Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you turn this into a full fictional episode told through a textile dye log, not a general story with a log stuck on afterward. it is for North Quay Textile Works, a small mill by the canal in Millhaven, and the shift is the evening of october 14. keep the writing practical and human, like several people are trying to leave a useful record for the next shift. the lot is D-418, work order WT-908, 240 kg of towel cloth that is 60 percent cotton and 40 percent linen. the requested color is warm slate blue. the story should stay with this one lot and this one shift rather than jumping forward to a later audit or explaining how the whole mill works.

Lila Moravec is the evening dye operator, Tomas Bell is the floor lead, and Inez Park works in the color lab. Lila has been at the mill six years and is careful with measurements, though she writes short notes when the floor is busy. Tomas has to coordinate the rinse room as well as the dye floor, so he keeps asking for times that the next shift can follow. use Kettle 3, which has a 1,200-liter working capacity. at 6:10 p.m. Lila checks the vessel tag and finds it clean, then records that the batch is loaded. the recipe for the lot is 18.6 kg reactive blue 19, 2.4 kg navy concentrate, 72 kg salt and 18 kg soda ash. the liquor ratio written on the work card is 1:8. the incoming water is 18 degrees celsius and the starting bath is 32 degrees after warming. put these details into the log naturally; they should read as real process notes, not like a shopping list pasted into the middle of the story. don't change the weights or the lot identifiers.

write the sequence from loading through dyeing and rinsing in time order. the salt goes in first and circulates for 12 minutes before the blue and navy are added. the color additions are made slowly over 8 minutes. soda ash is dissolved separately and added in two portions, 10 minutes apart. the bath is held at 32 degrees for 35 minutes after the second portion. the first pH check, after the second soda portion, is 10.8. at 7:24 the pump gives a brief uneven hum, but Lila checks the return flow and it steadies without stopping the run. mention that she notes the sound and that Tomas checks the pump housing; don't turn that into a breakdown or a repair.

make the dialogue ordinary and short. Lila says, “the blue is reading a little flat under this light.” Tomas answers, “don't chase the shade until the sample is dry.” Inez later says, “the second reading is for conductivity, not color.” keep the quotes as given and let them fit into the shift, rather than making them a dramatic argument. the wet sample looks darker than the dry one, which is why they wait for Inez's lab check. don't say the color is approved, rejected, or corrected; the log should report what was seen and measured.

please include a numbered section somewhere in the log, with these entries in this order:
1. 6:10 p.m. — lot D-418 loaded in Kettle 3; vessel tag checked and clean.
2. 6:22 p.m. — salt circulation complete; color additions begin.
3. 6:30 p.m. — blue and navy additions complete; soda ash solution prepared separately.
4. 6:40 p.m. — first soda portion added.
5. 6:50 p.m. — second soda portion added; pH 10.8.
6. 7:25 p.m. — return flow steady after the uneven pump hum; housing checked.
The entries can have surrounding prose, but keep the time and event details consistent with the sequence above. don't omit the number section just because there are other log notes.

at 8:12 p.m. the first rinse starts in Rinse Tank 2. at 8:32 the conductivity reading is 1.8 mS/cm. make the branch explicit: if the reading is at or below 1.5 mS/cm, move the lot to the hydro extractor; if it is above 1.5 mS/cm, keep it in the rinse tank and take another reading after 10 minutes. the recorded 1.8 means they keep it in the tank. at 8:42 the next reading is 1.3 mS/cm, so they move the lot to the hydro extractor. keep both sides of the condition in the prompt and make clear which side applies at each recorded reading. this condition should matter to what happens later, not just appear as a rule with no consequence.

include a few other grounded details from the shift: the rinse tank tag is blue and marked RT-2, the log sheet has a damp lower corner from a nearby hose, and Tomas asks Lila to write the extractor handoff time clearly because the morning crew starts at 6:00. the lot goes into the hydro extractor at 8:49 p.m.; do not invent a drying time or a next-morning result. Inez compares the dry lab swatch with the reference card at 9:05 and writes that the swatch is still being observed under the standard lamp. that is the last color note for this shift. no one decides what to do with the shade afterward.

end with a substantive final log paragraph at the end of the episode, not a summary or recommendation. it should record that the extractor handoff was entered at 8:49, the batch and work order numbers are on the slip, and the damp sheet was clipped to the shift board so the morning crew can find it. mention that Lila left the lab swatch beside the reference card for Inez, who was still there at 9:05. keep the ending within the information above, and leave the shade observation open without implying a later decision.", "output": "Write a complete fictional episode presented through the textile dye log for North Quay Textile Works, a small mill by the canal in Millhaven. Set it on the evening of October 14. Keep the practical, human tone of several people leaving a useful record for the next shift. Follow one lot through one shift; do not jump forward to a later audit or explain how the entire mill works.

### People and batch

Lila Moravec is the evening dye operator. She has worked at the mill for six years and is careful with measurements, though she writes short notes when the floor is busy. Tomas Bell is the floor lead and coordinates both the rinse room and dye floor, so he asks for times the next shift can follow. Inez Park works in the color lab beside the loading doors and is on site until 9:30 p.m. Show their work through log notes and brief exchanges rather than long biographies. They know one another and speak plainly, but no one is careless about the batch.

The lot is D-418, work order WT-908: 240 kg of towel cloth, 60 percent cotton and 40 percent linen, in the requested color warm slate blue. Keep the episode focused on this lot.

### Dyeing sequence

Use Kettle 3, with a 1,200-liter working capacity. At 6:10 p.m., Lila checks the vessel tag, finds it clean, and records that the batch is loaded. The recipe is 18.6 kg reactive blue 19, 2.4 kg navy concentrate, 72 kg salt, and 18 kg soda ash. The work card gives a liquor ratio of 1:8. Incoming water is 18 degrees Celsius, and the starting bath is 32 degrees after warming. Include these facts naturally as process notes, not as a pasted-in shopping list, and keep the weights and identifiers exact.

Write events in time order. Salt goes in first and circulates for 12 minutes before the blue and navy are added slowly over 8 minutes. Soda ash is dissolved separately and added in two portions 10 minutes apart. Hold the bath at 32 degrees for 35 minutes after the second portion. The first pH check, after the second soda portion, is 10.8. At 7:24 p.m., the pump gives a brief uneven hum. Lila checks the return flow and it steadies without stopping the run. She notes the sound, and Tomas checks the pump housing. Do not describe this as a breakdown or repair.

Include this numbered section in the log, in this order:
1. 6:10 p.m. — Lot D-418 loaded in Kettle 3; vessel tag checked and clean.
2. 6:22 p.m. — Salt circulation complete; color additions begin.
3. 6:30 p.m. — Blue and navy additions complete; soda ash solution prepared separately.
4. 6:40 p.m. — First soda portion added.
5. 6:50 p.m. — Second soda portion added; pH 10.8.
6. 7:25 p.m. — Return flow steady after the uneven pump hum; housing checked.

Surround the numbered entries with prose if useful, but keep their times and events consistent with the sequence. Do not omit the section.

### Rinse and color notes

Begin the first rinse in Rinse Tank 2 at 8:12 p.m. At 8:32 p.m., record a conductivity reading of 1.8 mS/cm and make the decision rule explicit: if the reading is at or below 1.5 mS/cm, move the lot to the hydro extractor; if it is above 1.5 mS/cm, keep it in the rinse tank and take another reading after 10 minutes. Since the recorded reading is 1.8 mS/cm, keep the lot in the tank. At 8:42 p.m., record 1.3 mS/cm and move the lot to the hydro extractor. Preserve both branches of the rule and show how the recorded readings determine the action.

Include a few grounded details from the shift: the rinse tank tag is blue and marked RT-2; the log sheet has a damp lower corner from a nearby hose; and Tomas asks Lila to write the extractor handoff time clearly because the morning crew starts at 6:00. The lot goes into the hydro extractor at 8:49 p.m. Do not invent a drying time or a next-morning result.

Use these short, ordinary exchanges exactly as given: Lila says, “the blue is reading a little flat under this light.” Tomas answers, “don't chase the shade until the sample is dry.” Inez later says, “the second reading is for conductivity, not color.” The wet sample looks darker than the dry one, which is why they wait for Inez's lab check. Keep the lines natural rather than turning them into a dramatic argument. At 9:05 p.m., Inez compares the dry lab swatch with the reference card and writes that the swatch is still being observed under the standard lamp. This is the last color note for the shift. Do not say the color is approved, rejected, or corrected, and do not imply a later decision about the shade.

End with a substantive final log paragraph, not a summary or recommendation. Record that the extractor handoff was entered at 8:49 p.m., that the batch and work order numbers are on the slip, and that the damp sheet was clipped to the shift board for the morning crew. Mention that Lila left the lab swatch beside the reference card for Inez, who was still there at 9:05 p.m. Keep the ending within these facts and leave the shade observation open."}]
